entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The Battle of Crécy was a pivotal engagement in the Hundred Years' War, fought on September 3, 1346, near the village of Crécy-en-Ponthieu in northern France. It was a decisive victory for the English army, led by King Edward III, over the French forces under the command of King Philip VI. This battle marked a significant shift in the balance of power in Western Europe, as the English gained control of the continent's northern regions. The English longbowmen played a crucial role in the battle, using their advanced ranged warfare tactics to devastating effect against the heavily armored French knights.

The consequences of the Battle of Crécy were far-reaching. It led to the English occupation of northern France, which lasted for over a century. The battle also marked the beginning of the end of the French monarchy's power and influence in Western Europe. The English victory at Crécy paved the way for the eventual rise of the English Empire in the 16th century.

One of the most lasting legacies of the Battle of Crécy is the impact it had on the development of military tactics and technology. The introduction of the longbow and its widespread adoption by the English army revolutionized the art of warfare, making it a key factor in the English victories at Agincourt and other battles in the Hundred Years' War. The English longbowmen became a formidable force on the battlefield, feared by their enemies for their accuracy and range.

In the words of historian Michael Jones, 'The Battle of Crécy was a turning point in the Hundred Years' War, marking a decisive shift in the balance of power in Western Europe and setting the stage for the English occupation of northern France.'
